papers.title_in_file: Automatic design of quantum feature maps
papers.version_note: arXiv:2105.12626v1 [quant-ph], 26 May 2021; text matches the record.
papers.what_it_is: A preprint proposing an NSGA-II genetic algorithm that designs quantum feature-map circuits for quantum kernel SVM classification, tested on a synthetic Moons set and three benchmark datasets.

existing.note: The abstract and Section 3.2 agree; Section 3.2.2 adds that the fitness is computed on a held-out test set.
existing.value: The authors propose an NSGA-II multiobjective genetic algorithm that automatically generates ansatze for QSVM classification, maximizing accuracy and minimizing ansatz size.
quotes: This efficient method is based on NSGA-II multiobjective genetic algorithms which allow both maximize the accuracy and minimize the ansatz size.

existing.note: Matches Section 4.3 (p. 11). The paper does not say which of the two uncorrelated circuits belong to which dataset beyond the Fig. 6 caption: (a) Parkinson, (b) drug classification, (c) IoT irrigation.
existing.value: The authors report that two of the generated circuits for the three benchmark problems are uncorrelated and have no CNOT gates, the third has just one entangler gate, and that such structures admit an efficient classical simulation.
quotes: two of the circuits are uncorrelated and have no CNOT gates, while the third one, for multiclass drug classification, has just one entangler gate
admit an efficient classical simulation which constitutes in itself a type of quantum-inspired machine-learning technique

existing.note: The stored value gives the setup and the validation set size but not the validation result: the paper reports 473 of 500 validation points correct (0.946), against 1.0 on the 30% test set.
existing.value: On a 150-point Moons synthetic non-linear dataset the 150 points are split 70% training and 30% test, the final circuit is reported at 1.0 accuracy in the figure caption, and the authors validated the model with a set of 500 additional points generated by the same synthetic algorithm. The authors report that 473 out of 500 validation points were correctly classified, which they state as 0.946 accuracy.
quotes: The 150 datapoints are scaled between [-1,+1] as a preprocessing step, and randomly split into a training (70%) and test (30%) sets.
(d) Final circuit with 1.0 accuracy.
We validate the utility of the model using additional datapoints, a validation set, with 500 points generated by the same synthetic algorithm.
because 473 out of 500 data in the dataset have been correctly classified.
a 94.6% of correct classified data or 0.946 accuracy.
existing.reader_inference: The 1.0 accuracy is on the test set that also drives the fitness (Section 3.2.2), so the 0.946 on fresh data is the only figure in the paper that was not used for selection. The drop from 1.0 to 0.946 is the generalization gap the authors do not discuss as such.

assertions.value: The authors state that they use a quantum kernel equal to the real part of the overlap of two feature states, not the squared overlap used in the cited prior work, and that they confirmed numerically that this kernel allows sharper separations and easier convergence of the optimizer.
quotes: In this work we use a diﬀerent type of quantum kernel

By not squaring the scalar product between vectors, the function resembles more the original motivation for K(x, x ). Moreover, as we have conﬁrmed numerically, this kernel allows for sharper separations and more easy convergence of the optimizer.
assertions.reader_inference: No numerical comparison of the two kernels is shown in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the real-part kernel is neutral from a classical simulation point of view but more complicated to evaluate on a quantum computer, where an ancillary qubit prepared in a superposition and controlling the operation U would be needed to estimate the scalar product by interference.
quotes: However, while this choice is neutral from a classical simulation point of view, it is more complicated to evaluate in a quantum computer.
we would need to use an ancillary qubit, prepared in a quantum superposition, and controlling the U operation, to estimate the scalar product as the result of an interference process.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2 (p. 4) states the limit in the authors' own words.
assertions.reader_inference: All reported results are classical simulations of the kernel; no run on quantum hardware is reported.

assertions.value: The authors encode a feature map as a bit string of size M x N x 5 for M qubits and a maximum of N layers, using five bits per gene; the i-th gene acts on qubit j = i mod M and may depend on input variable k = i mod d, with genes applied in sequential order.
quotes: The process starts with an initial population of individuals, represented by bit strings of size M × N × 5.
we use ﬁve bits per gene s0s1s2s3s4
with j = i mod M and k = i mod d.

assertions.value: The authors state that the first three bits of a gene select a fixed gate (Hadamard or CNOT) or a local rotation parameterized by an input value, that the rotation axis is chosen by those bits, that the last two bits select a proportionality parameter, that a CNOT acts on consecutive qubits j and j + 1 mod M, and that all other bit combinations are identity operations.
quotes: The mapping from bits to gates is also very straightforward.
the last two bits select a proportionality parameter
When the gate is a CNOT, it acts on consequitive qubits, j and j + 1 mod M.
All other combinations of bits not reﬂected in ﬁgure 1b are taken to be just identity operations.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.2.1 (p. 6) defines the mapping; the exact bit table is in Fig. 1b, not in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The formula for the proportionality parameter theta_i is garbled in the text layer, so it is not entered here.

assertions.value: The authors define a size metric SM that gives different costs to local and entangling gates, with CNOT gates counted twice: SizeMetric(SM) = Nlocal + 2NCNOT.
quotes: we introduce a size metric, labeled SM, which assigns diﬀerent costs to the number of local gates
SizeMetric(SM) = Nlocal + 2NCNOT
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the term Nqubits under the equation; it appears to be a denominator, but this is a reading of the layout.

assertions.value: The authors define the multiobjective fitness function WeightsControl(WC) = SM + SM times accuracy squared (the exponent prints flat as accuracy2), which increases the relevance of SM as the accuracy approaches its limiting value 1.
quotes: we engineer a ﬁtness function that increases the relevance of the SM as the accuracy approaches its limiting value 1
WeightsControl(WC) = SM + SM ∗ accuracy2.

assertions.value: The authors state that the data are divided into a training set and a test set, that the classifier is built on the training set, and that the accuracy used in the fitness is estimated over the test set as the fraction of points properly classified.
quotes: To compute this metric, we divide the data into a training set and a test set.
We then estimate the accuracy of the model f (x) over the test set, as the fraction of points that are properly classiﬁed.
assertions.reader_inference: The test set therefore guides selection of the circuit, so the 1.0 accuracies in Fig. 3d and Table 1 are on data that shaped the search. Only the 500-point Moons validation set was held out from the search.

assertions.value: The authors state that selection uses the multiobjective algorithm NSGA-II, which decides survivors by Pareto dominance and density-based metrics, and that elitism is increased with a Mu Plus Lambda strategy in which the current population (size mu) competes with the offspring (lambda).
quotes: The selection operator is a multiobjetive Non-Sorted Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II).
This algorithm decides which individuals survive to the next generation based on Pareto-dominance and density-based metrics
We increase the elitism of the algorithm with a Mu Plus Lambda (µ + λ) algorithm.

assertions.value: The authors state that mutation is a bit flip with probability pmut per individual and pind per gene, and that crossover is a binary swap of contiguous bit substrings applied with probability pcross, with the swap endpoints chosen at random.
quotes: Since our feature maps are coded in binary format, we can use a bit ﬂip mutation operator
we implement a binary swap of contiguous bit substrings
The value pcross determines probability that a crossover takes place

assertions.value: The authors report that after several tests the optimal hyperparameters were 30% probability of crossover and 70% mutation, with a 20% probability of bits being mutated.
quotes: After several tests, the optimal hyperparameters were found to be 30% probability of crossover and 70% mutation, with a 20% probability of bits being mutated.
assertions.reader_inference: No tuning data is shown. The same values are used for all datasets in Table 1.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the Moons toy problem they trained circuits with up to 6 qubits and 6 layers, optimized over 5000 generations with a population of 100 individuals.
quotes: These sets are used to train quantum circuits with up to 6 qubits and 6 layers
we optimize the circuits over 5000 generations, using a population of 100 individuals.

assertions.value: The authors report that the Pareto front with elitist strategies led to a circuit with no entanglement, and that after 5000 generations the algorithm produced the simple uncorrelated circuit of Fig. 3d, which fits the test set with perfect accuracy.
quotes: no entanglement at all is required to ﬁt this model
Thus, after 5000 generations, the algorithm produces the simple uncorrelated circuit
from ﬁgure 3d, which ﬁts the test set with perfect accuracy.
assertions.reader_inference: Perfect accuracy here is on the test set that also drives the fitness.

assertions.value: The authors state that even the initial circuits show a penalty on CNOT gates, with fewer entangling unitaries than other ansatze in the literature.
quotes: Already in these circuits we observe the penalty associated to CNOT gates decreasing the number of entangling unitaries, as compared to other ansa¨tze in the literature.
assertions.reader_inference: No comparison with other ansatze is shown.

assertions.value: The authors report that the confusion matrix on the 500-point validation set shows 473 of 500 points correctly classified, and conclude that the QSVM extrapolates to unseen data from the same distribution.
quotes: The confusion matrix allows us to conclude that the QSVM extrapolates to unseen data with same distribution
473 out of 500 data in the dataset have been correctly classiﬁed.
assertions.reader_inference: The distribution is a synthetic one with a fixed generator. No confidence interval or repeat run is reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that the strong penalty on entangling gates makes the algorithm prefer circuits with smaller clusters of uncorrelated qubits, so that the circuit is a tensor product of separate unitaries and the quantum kernel is a product of separate kernels, K(x, x') as a product over i of Ki(x, x').
quotes: the strong penalty on entangling gates makes the genetic algorithm prefer circuits that have smaller clusters of uncorrelated qubits
The result is a circuit that can be decomposed as a tensor product of separate
unitaries, and a quantum kernel that is a scalar product of separate kernels

assertions.value: The authors report for the Moons circuit that the full kernel has accuracy 1.0 and the single-qubit kernels have lower accuracies of 0.57, 0.68 and 0.53 (qubits one to three, Fig. 5b-d), with qubits one and two giving linear hyperplanes and qubit three giving non-linearity through three rotations.
quotes: 5a illustrates the boundaries of the complete kernel, which has accuracy 1.0
the single-qubit boundaries have a lower classiﬁcation accuracy, of 0.57, 0.68 and 0.53, respectively
qubits one and two, provide linear hyperplanes, being qubit three the one that provides a degree of non-linearity achieved by applying three rotations.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not say whether Fig. 5 accuracies are on the training, test or validation data; 1.0 matches the test set (Fig. 3d), not the 0.946 validation figure.

assertions.value: The authors report applying the method to three other benchmark problems (Parkinson, IoT irrigation, drug classification), listed in Table 1 with dataset characteristics, genetic-algorithm hyperparameters and resulting accuracy, and state that the technique performs well for datasets with many features and for more than two classes.
quotes: Table 1 lists three problems, with the characteristics of the datasets, the hyperparameters of the genetic algorithm and the resulting accuracy.
the technique performs well for datasets with a high number of features as well as for datasets with more than two classes.
assertions.reader_inference: The table cells print one per line in the text layer and cannot be quoted. The brief's reading of Table 1 is: genetic-algorithm accuracy 1.0 on all three problems.

assertions.value: The authors state that the comparison with the classical k-NN, linear SVM and degree-2 polynomial SVM shows an advantage of the QSVM technique, especially in the multiclass classification of drugs.
quotes: The comparison with non-quantum classiﬁcation methods also shows and advantage of the QSVM technique, specially in the highly complex multiclass classiﬁcation of drugs.
a k-NN, a linear support vector machine, and an SVM with a polynomial kernel with degree 2
assertions.reader_inference: Per Table 1 as printed, the classical methods reach 1.0 on the IoT problem, equal to the QSVM; the Parkinson baselines are below 1.0. The quantum accuracy is on test data used in the fitness, the baselines are not stated to be tuned or cross-validated, and no repeated runs are reported, so the comparison is not like for like.

assertions.value: The authors state that the evolved structures, with little or no correlation, admit an efficient classical simulation, which they describe as a type of quantum-inspired machine-learning technique, and that they attribute this to the classification power of single qubits as in an earlier cited work.
quotes: First, it illustrates the power of individual qubits a quantum classiﬁers, a realization already introduced in Ref. [32].
We attribute the simplicity of these circuits to the classiﬁcation power of single qubits and single-qubit operations [32]
assertions.reader_inference: If the circuits are classically simulable, the reported accuracies do not show a quantum advantage; the paper does not claim one.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the algorithm produces 100% accurate classifiers that can still generalize to unseen data since the metric is obtained from test sets, and that product states may serve as another quantum-inspired variational strategy.
quotes: The algorithm produces 100% accurate classiﬁers that can still generalize to unseen data since this metric is obtained from test sets.
our results suggest the power of product states as another quantum-inspired variational strategy for supervised learning.
assertions.reader_inference: The test sets also drive the fitness, so 'unseen' holds only for the Moons validation set (0.946), not for the 1.0 values.

assertions.value: The authors state that they believe the resulting circuits are amenable to interpretation in a simpler way than neural networks or other ML ansatze.
quotes: We believe that the resulting circuits are amenable to further interpretation strategies, in a simpler way than neural networks or other ML ansa¨tze.

assertions.value: The authors list future directions: enlarging the set of weights in the parameterization, changing the order of parameters, adding more local and entangling gates, adding free parameters optimized with SPSA or other strategies, and developing rule-based explanation of entanglement-free models.
quotes: This can be extended in various ways, such as enlarging the set of weights in the parameterization
including free parameters θi that can be optimized using SPSA or other strategies
developing a kind of rule-based explanation of the model.

assertions.value: The authors state that their gene encoding contains a minimalistic set of entangling, local and parameterized gates, with sufficient precision for the problems explored.
quotes: The gene encoding that we have implemented contains a minimalistic set of entangling, local and parameterized gates
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 5 (p. 13) states the scope of the encoding.
